p: brethren: The first: charity which proceeds from a true faith, cannot exist with the respecting of people: which he proves plainly by using the example of those who, while having reproach or disdain for the poor, honour the rich.
glory: For if we knew what Christ's glory is, and esteemed it as we should, there would not be the respecting of people that there is.
good place: In a worshipful and honourable place.
yourselves: Have you not within yourselves judged one man to be preferred over another (which you should not do) by means of this?
Hearken: He shows that those who prefer the rich over the poor are wicked and disobedient judges, since God on the other hand prefers the poor (whom he has enriched with true riches) over the rich.
poor of this world rich in: The needy and wretched, and (if we measure it after the opinion of the world) the most degraded of all men.

Do not rich men oppress you: Secondly, he proves them to be fools: since the rich men are rather to be held detestable and cursed, considering that they persecute the church, and blaspheme Christ: for he speaks of wicked and profane rich men, as most of them have always been, beside whom he contrasts the poor and degraded.
called: Literally, "which is called upon of you".
If ye fulfil the: The conclusion: charity which God prescribes cannot agree with the respecting of people, seeing that we must walk in the king's highway.

royal law according to the scripture: The law is said to be royal and like the king's highway, in that it is simple and without changes, and that the law calls everyone our neighbour without respect, whom we may help by any kind of duty.

For whosoever shall keep the whole: A new argument to prove the same conclusion: Those who neglect some and ambitiously honour others do not love their neighbours. For they do not obey God if they remove from the commandments of God those things that are not convenient for them. Rather they are guilty of breaking the whole law, even though they observe part of it.
all: Not that all sins are equal, but because he who breaks one small part of the law, offends the majority of the given law.
For he that said: A proof: because the Lawmaker is always one and the same, and the contents of the law cannot be divided.

So speak ye: The conclusion of the whole treatise: we are upon this condition delivered from the curse of the law by the mercy of God, that in the same way we should maintain and cherish charity and good will towards one another, and whoever does not do so, shall not taste of the grace of God.
mercy: He that is harsh and short with his neighbour, or else does not help him, he shall find God a hard and rough judge to him.

What doth it profit: The fifth place which follows very well with the former treatise, concerning a true and living faith. The proposition of the place is this: Faith which does not bring forth works is not that faith by means of which we are justified, but an false image of that faith, or else this: they who do not show the effects of faith are not justified by faith.

If a brother or sister be: The first reason taken from a comparison: if a man says to one who is hungry "Fill your belly" and yet gives him nothing, this is not true charity. If a man says he believes and does not bring forth works of his faith, this is not true faith, but truly a dead thing called with the name of faith, of which no man has room to brag, unless he will openly incur reprehension, since the cause is understood by the effects.
a man may say: No, by this every man will be eaten up with pride.

Thou believest that there is one: Another reason taken from an absurdity: if such a faith were the true faith by means of which we are justified, the demons would be justified, for they have that, but nonetheless they tremble and are not justified, therefore neither is that faith a true faith.

But wilt thou know: The third reason from the example of Abraham, who no doubt had a true faith: but he in offering his son, showed himself to have that faith which was not without works, and therefore he received a true testimony when it was laid, that faith was imputed to him for righteousness.
justified by works: Was he not by his works known and found to be justified? For he speaks not here of the causes of justification, but by what effects we may know that a man is justified.
wrought with his works: Was effectual and fruitful with good works.
perfect: That the faith was declared to be a true faith, through works.
fulfilled which saith: Then the Scripture was fulfilled, when it appeared plainly how truly it was written about Abraham.
Ye see then how that by: The conclusion: Only he who has faith that has works following it is justified.
justified: Is proved to be just.
faith only: Of that dead and fruitless faith which you boast of.
Likewise also was not Rahab the: A forth reason taken from a similar example of Rahab the harlot, who was proved by her works that she was justified by a true faith.
For as the body without the: The conclusion repeated again: faith does not bring forth fruits and works is not faith, but a dead carcass.
